title: Evaluating Verified Autonomy in Quantum Engineering
authors: Naixu Guo, Changhao Li, Siyu Cheng, Qicheng Tang, Binzhao Luo, Bikun Li, Yuxuan Du, Shihao Ru, Jiaqi Cai
abstract: Reliable quantum engineering is essential for turning quantum phenomena into practical technologies. As quantum platforms grow in scale and complexity, their characterization and operation require increasing human effort and coordination. Scientific artificial intelligence agents, which can plan experiments, operate instruments, and analyze observations, offer a promising route towards autonomous quantum engineering. Yet whether current agents can perform reliably in this setting has not been systematically established. To fill this gap, we developed Quantum-Harbor, a virtual laboratory that provides a controlled execution environment for agents to interact with quantum systems. This design enables direct verification of both the actions taken and the conclusions drawn. Building on this framework, we introduce QIQCBench, a benchmark of $49$ expert-authored tasks spanning multiple layers including calibration and control, error correction and compilation, sensing and networking. Across $17$ frontier agentic systems, QIQCBench reveals wide variation in verified performance. These results expose a substantial gap between demonstrating capability and achieving reliable operation, and establish Quantum-Harbor as a foundation for measuring progress towards verified autonomy in quantum engineering.
summary: This paper introduces Quantum-Harbor, a virtual laboratory, and QIQCBench, a comprehensive benchmark to test AI agents in quantum engineering. It moves beyond simple testing by requiring agents to prove their results by recomputing them from raw data. The work highlights that while agents can show capability, achieving reliable, verified autonomy in complex quantum workflows remains a significant challenge.
main_problem: The core problem is systematically evaluating the reliable, end-to-end performance of scientific AI agents in complex, multi-stage quantum engineering workflows.
main_result: The benchmark reveals a substantial gap between an agent's demonstrated capability and its ability to achieve reliable, verified operation in real-world quantum tasks.
method: The authors developed Quantum-Harbor, a virtual lab, and QIQCBench, a benchmark of 49 expert tasks, to rigorously test agents' ability to plan, execute, and verify results from raw data.
model_or_system: The system involves simulating various quantum platforms (transmon, trapped ion, etc.) within the Quantum-Harbor framework. Agents interact with this environment to perform tasks like logical CNOT gate operations and surrogate model fitting.
key_observables: Per-cycle error rates (e.g., $	ext{error} < 10^{-3}$), Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) for model prediction, and overall task pass/fail rates.
important_parameters: The benchmark covers multiple layers of the quantum stack, including calibration, error correction, and compilation.
main_assumptions: The evaluation relies on a 'sidecar' component and an evidence-bound grader to ensure results are verifiable against the raw execution log, preventing agents from cheating.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the agent workflow (plan $	o$ run $	o$ analyze $	o$ adapt), the architecture of Quantum-Harbor (agent environment, sidecar, evidence log), and the structure of QIQCBench across various quantum computing layers.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the necessity of autonomous quantum engineering, details the Quantum-Harbor framework and QIQCBench benchmark, presents results showing performance gaps, and establishes the framework for measuring verified autonomy.
why_interesting: It provides a novel, rigorous testing ground for AI agents interacting with quantum hardware simulations, which is crucial for advancing practical quantum computation beyond theoretical models.
